newsitem.title: UKRAINE: FEATURE - Investment funds take fresh look at Ukraine.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Investment funds take fresh look at Ukraine.

text.p: KIEV, Feb 25 Reuter) - Investment funds keen to repeat the high returns they enjoyed in Russia are starting to turn their attention to Ukraine, but some analysts observing the trend say gains might not be as high as expected.

"Russia has already had its day in the sun. People are looking for new places. Some people think it will be Ukraine," said Maryna Hrushetska, an analyst with the European Privatisation Investment Corporation (EPIC).

She said her company, an Austrian investment bank which launched Ukraine's first foreign capital fund in 1994, has witnessed not just a recent increase in calls from institutional clients, but also growth in committed capital.

Regent Pacific, the Hong Kong and London-based fund management group, has announced plans to close a new $50 million Ukraine investment fund next month, and Caspian Securities Inc is also expected to follow with a fund of about the same size.
Regent Fund Manager Andrew Leasor said the fund will invest in about 20 industrial sector firms which he described as "bluer chip companies", in the country of 52 million.
"A lot of people missed out on the early days in Russia and they don't want to do that here," Leasor said. "This is seen as the last great investment frontier in Europe."
PRIVATISATION DRAGGING
But Ukraine may not be as similar to Russia as investors think. Despite monetary stability and slower inflation, privatisation has been slow, Hrushetska said.
"Fund managers want to replicate the success they had in Russia, but unlike Russia the big assets have not been privatised," she said.
"People say we have $50 million, what can we buy -- the untapped equity market is nothing like on the scale of Russia," she said. "Every investor wants undervalued assets and long-term growth."

Ukraine has attracted only $1.2 billion in private investment since independence in 1991 -- a situation which recently caused Deputy Prime Minister Viktor Pynzenyk to angrily remark that despite reforms, "Nothing is happening."
Hrushetska said another drawback is that Ukraine is not yet predicting economic growth, and predicted that 1997 would be more a year of steady progress than of economic boom.
INTEREST INCREASING
Ukraine has nearly finished selling off small businesses and is proceeding with medium- and large-scale privatisation, including enterprises deemed strategic to national security.

But to date it can name only Ukrainsky Richkovy Flot (Ukrrechflot), the country's largest shipping firm, as a large-scale privatisation success story. Power company privatisation should start only at the end of this year.
The embryonic Ukrainian Stock Exchange, which convenes once a week, lists about 20 companies and has such a tiny turnover that some weeks no trading takes place.
"Ukrainian brokers put prices on the screen just to see if anyone is there," Leasor said of the slightly more active over-the-counter market.

But Bogdan Kotchoubey, an investment manager with the Swiss private bank Pictet, said his company's First Russian Frontiers Trust had invested in 11 companies in Ukraine and despite the overall risks, some companies are worth banking on.
"Interest in Ukraine will go up," he said. "There are some very good companies that are valued very cheaply."
Ukraine already has one or two country-specific funds, and analysts predict more and more investment companies will try their luck here.
"There's a lemming-like effect," said Kempton Jenkins of the Ukraine-U.S. Business Council, a joint group set up to promote private investment in the former Soviet republic.
EUROBOND CREDIBILITY

"The first wave of East European countries are coming close to West European countries, and interest is increasing in Ukraine," said Kay Haigh, a senior economist for emerging markets at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.
Haigh said the fall in Treasury bill yields to about 40 percent now from 100 percent a year ago has pushed investors towards other local markets.
Ukraine would gain extra credibility with a planned Eurobond issue expected in the first or second quarter, Haigh said.
"In 1997 Ukraine will want to put itself on the international investment map and will do that with the Eurobond," Haigh said. "Ukraine will become more attractive to investors."
Investors in Ukraine faced typical emerging market risks such as currency, convertibility and default, he said.
"But given the level of T-bill yields, and the Eurobond, investors see manageable risk," Haigh added.
